newsitem.title: UK: UK March CIPS Report on Services-full text.
newsitem.headline: UK March CIPS Report on Services-full text.

text.p: The new CIPS monthly survey of the UK services economy found a significant increase in business activity in March with employment growing at an accelerating rate in response to strong growth of new business. The survey is based on a panel of 500 UK business executives in private sector service industries (excluding retail and wholesale). Indexes are calculated to measure the direction of change of business conditions, such that readings above 50.0 indicate expansion and below 50.0 contraction. The greater the divergence from 50.0, the greater the rate of change indicated.

The seasonally adjusted Business Activity Index, at a level significantly higher than 50.0 since the survey began last July, has therefore recorded a sharp expansion of activity over the past nine months with an acceleration of the rate of growth in March. Over 35% of all companies reported an increase in business activity while just 9% reported a decline. This strong growth of activity reflects increasing amounts of new business being placed with service sector companies: March saw the largest increase in new business recorded since the survey began.

A consequence of this growth of incoming new business has been a rise in the amount of work outstanding (or work in hand). Employment rose strongly again -- the ninth consecutive rise -- in response to the need to increase capacity to meet further growth of demand: in March, three quarters of all companies expected the level of business activity at their company to be higher in a year's time. Only 6.0 percent expected a decline. Such buoyant confidence has now been evident for nine months running.

However, the ability of firms to boost capacity to meet demand has been increasingly hindered by a lack of resources in recent months -- notably a lack of highly skilled personnel. With the labour market continuing to tighten, rising wages and salaries were found to have been the principal cause of a further increase in costs during March. Prices charged by panel members for their services rose for the fifth consecutive month as the recent growth in demand has allowed an increasing number of companies to pass these higher costs onto their customers. However, the total proportion of all firms raising their charges remained modest at just over 10 percent in March.

After seasonal adjustment, the Incoming New Business Index rose to 62.4 in March. This is the highest index reading yet recorded by this survey and suggests a considerable increase in demand for services. The amount of new business placed was found to have risen in 36% of companies. The growth in demand over the past nine months has generally been attributed simply to the improved economic climate, which a growing number of firms have taken advantage of through greater sales and marketing activity.

Panel members reported a sharp rise in the amount of outstanding business in March (defined as work in hand but not yet undertaken). The seasonally adjusted rate at which outstanding business has been growing has risen steadily since last December. In the majority of cases, the build up of work just reflects the strength at which new business has grown in recent months. However, in an increasing number of cases, the ability to meet growth of demand has been hindered by a lack of resources.

The seasonally adjusted Employment Index rose further above the 50.0 level in March, signalling an increase in the rate of growth. A quarter of all companies, spread across all key service sectors, reported higher staffing levels in March. Less than 10 percent reported lower levels, a quarter of which were resignations rather than redundancies. Employment has risen in each month since the survey started last July as firms have increased capacity to meet growth of new business.

Prices charged by panel member companies rose modestly for the fifth consecutive month in March. Until last November charges were generally found to have been falling as weak demand for services led companies to compete for new business on price. The subsequent modest rise in prices charged has been associated with rising costs and hardening demand. Nevertheless, competition remained strong in March and continued to limit the rate of growth of charges with only 10% of firms able to raise prices.

The seasonally adjusted Input Prices Index remained well above the 50.0 "no change" level in March and thereby indicated a further sharp rise. Prices have risen throughout the nine month history of this survey and the rate of growth has picked up since last summer. The principal "input" to service sector activities is labour and the rise in the index largely reflects higher wages, a key cause of which has been a tightening of the labour market over the past nine months, especially for highly skilled professions.

Three quarters of all panel members expect their companies' business activity levels to rise over the next year. This buoyancy of business confidence has been seen throughout the past nine months with increasing numbers of firms planning to expand capacity and launch new products. The Expectations Index dipped very slightly as the number of firms expecting business to deteriorate following the election rose modestly. However, accounting for less than six percent of the panel, these firms remain very much exceptions. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
